report.summary: Measured evidence in SWE-bench Lite shows ReAct agents (SWE-agent 18%, Agentless 27%) outperform plan-then-execute baselines (~5-10%). Rigid decomposition hurts when dynamic feedback is needed; tree search benefits reasoning but limited coding gains. Decomposition helps only if plans are iteratively refined with execution feedback.
risks: Comparisons are confounded by different tool interfaces and model capabilities; exact numbers are uncertain and based on recall of evolving leaderboards.
Plan-then-execute includes a spectrum from naive single‑step decompose‑to‑the‑end to iterated refinement; simple ablation may not capture the nuance.
Tree‑search evidence is largely from reasoning tasks (e.g., Game of 24, Creative Writing) with few rigorous coding‑task studies.
Fabrication risk: names like "SWE-agent" and percentages are from memory, not verified against current publications.
todos: Re‑read the SWE-agent paper to confirm if they measured a decomposed baseline.
Audit the SWE-bench Lite leaderboard for up‑to‑date resolve rates.
Design a head‑to‑head experiment: same LLM, same agent scaffold, vary only the decomposition‑then‑execute vs. ReAct strategy.
Search for any coding‑focused tree‑search paper (e.g., MCTS for code repair) and extract quantitative comparisons.

handoff.suggestion: Run a controlled ablation on SWE-bench Lite (or a 100‑task subset) with GPT‑4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet: compare (a) single upfront decomposition into subtasks then sequential execution (no revisiting the plan), (b) ReAct loop that dynamically decides the next action, (c) iterative plan‑and‑execute that revisits the plan after each step. Measure resolve rate and plan‑adherence; publish the exact difference. This will ground future architecture decisions in measured evidence rather than extrapolation from reasoning tasks.
